config.title: Auth Context

intro.title: Auth Context
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a secure way to manage user authentication state across your React application using the Context API. You will create an 'Auth Context' that provides login status and user information to any component that needs it, without manually passing props down the component tree. The core concept is React's Context, which allows you to share data globally, combined with TypeScript for type-safe state and functions. You'll implement a context provider, custom hooks, and update the UI based on the authentication state. By the end, you'll have a reusable auth system that keeps your components clean and your user state consistent.
intro.usecase: Auth Context is essential for managing user authentication state across entire React applications, appearing in virtually every product requiring login functionality. You'll see this pattern in e-commerce platforms where user profile data needs to be accessible from the header, cart, and checkout pages simultaneously. Dashboard applications use Auth Context to conditionally render admin panels or user-specific content based on authentication status. Social media apps rely on it to maintain user sessions while navigating between feeds, profiles, and messaging interfaces. This centralized approach prevents prop drilling and ensures consistent authentication state management throughout complex applications.

objectives: Apply the createContext function to initialize a new authentication context in TypeScript
Define a TypeScript interface to specify the shape of the authentication context value
Implement a custom provider component to wrap the application and manage authentication state
Use the useState hook to store and update authentication status and user data
Construct context provider props to pass children components through the authentication wrapper
Access the authentication context in child components using the useContext hook
Execute conditional rendering based on authentication state to control UI visibility
Handle authentication actions (login/logout) through context methods that update the shared state
Utilize TypeScript generics with createContext to ensure type safety throughout the application
Return appropriate JSX from the provider component to make the context available to its children
Modify component structure to consume authentication state without prop drilling
Assign default values to the authentication context to prevent runtime errors in consuming components

steps.title: Import React and createContext from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the createContext function from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use a named import to bring in both React and createContext from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and createContext
import React, { createContext } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and createContext from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The 'react' package is imported with React and createContext available for use.
successCriteria: The code includes an import statement that imports both React and createContext from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and createContext from the 'react' package. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the ability to create context objects.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement isn't quite complete. Make sure you're importing both React and createContext from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import both React and createContext from the 'react' package to proceed.

steps.title: Import useContext from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import the useContext hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Add an import statement that brings in useContext from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing useContext from 'react'
import { useContext } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The useContext hook will be available to consume context values later in the component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported useContext from 'react'. This hook will allow components to access context values.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing 'useContext' specifically from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import the useContext hook from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Define the AuthContext interface
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named 'AuthContextType' with two properties: 'isAuthenticated' (boolean) and 'login' (function that takes no arguments and returns void).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions. Remember to specify the types for each property.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a TypeScript interface that defines the shape of your authentication context, specifying that it must contain an authentication status and a login function.
successCriteria: The code includes an interface named 'AuthContextType' with 'isAuthenticated: boolean' and 'login: () => void' properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the AuthContextType interface with the correct property types. This interface will ensure type safety when using the authentication context throughout your application.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be an issue with the interface definition. Make sure you have both properties with the correct types: 'isAuthenticated' should be a boolean, and 'login' should be a function that returns void.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition doesn't match the requirements. You need to create an interface named 'AuthContextType' with 'isAuthenticated: boolean' and 'login: () => void' properties. Check your syntax and property types.

steps.title: Create the AuthContext with createContext
steps.instruction: Use the imported createContext function to create a context named AuthContext. Provide it with an initial value of undefined and explicitly type it with the AuthContext interface you defined.
steps.hint: Call createContext<AuthContextType>(undefined). This creates a React context object with the correct type.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a properly typed AuthContext created with createContext, ready to be used as a provider and consumer.
successCriteria: The code must include a call to createContext with the generic type AuthContextType | undefined and an initial value of undefined.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the AuthContext with the correct type and initial value. This context will serve as the foundation for sharing authentication state throughout your app.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there's something missing. Make sure you're using createContext with the AuthContextType interface and providing undefined as the initial value.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look quite right. Remember to use createContext<AuthContextType | undefined>(undefined) to create your context with the proper typing.

steps.title: Create the AuthProvider component
steps.instruction: Define a functional component named AuthProvider that takes children as props. The component should return the children prop for now.
steps.hint: Create a function or arrow function called AuthProvider with a children prop parameter. Return children directly.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a basic AuthProvider component that accepts children and returns them.
successCriteria: The code includes a functional component named AuthProvider that takes a children prop and returns it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the AuthProvider component. This will serve as the wrapper that provides authentication state to your app.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined a component named AuthProvider that accepts children as a prop and returns it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The AuthProvider component is not defined correctly. Check that you've created a function named AuthProvider with a children prop and returned it.

steps.title: Initialize isAuthenticated state in AuthProvider
steps.instruction: Inside the AuthProvider component, initialize a state variable called 'isAuthenticated' using the useState hook. Set its initial value to false.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook to create a boolean state variable. Remember to import useState if you haven't already.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a boolean state variable
const [isVisible, setIsVisible] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: The AuthProvider component now has an isAuthenticated state variable initialized to false.
successCriteria: Initial value is set to false
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the isAuthenticated state variable with the correct initial value.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you use useState? Is the variable named 'isAuthenticated'? Is the initial value false? Did you specify the boolean type?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Inside AuthProvider, use useState to create a boolean state variable called 'isAuthenticated' with initial value false.

steps.title: Define the login function in AuthProvider
steps.instruction: Inside the AuthProvider component, define a function named 'login' that sets the isAuthenticated state to true.
steps.hint: Create a function that calls the setter function for isAuthenticated with the value true.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AuthProvider component now has a login function that will update the authentication state when called.
successCriteria: The login function is defined inside AuthProvider, calls setIsAuthenticated(true), and matches the signature from the AuthContextType interface.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the login function that sets isAuthenticated to true.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a login function, but make sure it calls setIsAuthenticated(true) to properly update the state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The login function is not properly defined. It should be inside AuthProvider and call setIsAuthenticated(true).

steps.title: Create the context value object
steps.instruction: Inside the AuthProvider component, create a value object that contains the isAuthenticated state and login function, matching the AuthContextType interface.
steps.hint: Create a constant variable named 'value' that's an object with properties isAuthenticated and login.
steps.expectedOutcome: A value object containing isAuthenticated and login properties is created inside the AuthProvider component.
successCriteria: The code should include a constant named 'value' (or similar) that's an object with properties isAuthenticated and login, referencing the existing state and function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the context value object with the required properties.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your value object includes both isAuthenticated and login properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The value object wasn't created correctly. Create an object containing isAuthenticated and login properties.

steps.title: Return the AuthContext.Provider with value
steps.instruction: In the AuthProvider component, return the AuthContext.Provider with the context value object and children as content.
steps.hint: Use the AuthContext.Provider component and pass the value prop containing the context object you will create. Remember to render the children inside the provider.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AuthProvider component now returns the AuthContext.Provider with the context value and children, making the authentication state available to all child components.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully returned the AuthContext.Provider with the context value, making the authentication state available to all child components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're returning AuthContext.Provider with both the value prop and children rendered inside it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The AuthProvider component should return AuthContext.Provider with the context value and children. Check that you're using the correct syntax for returning JSX.

steps.title: Create a custom useAuth hook
steps.instruction: Define a custom hook named useAuth that uses useContext with AuthContext and returns the context value. Add this hook after the AuthProvider component.
steps.hint: Create a function that calls useContext with AuthContext and returns its value. Make sure to handle the case where the context might be undefined.
steps.expectedOutcome: A custom hook named useAuth is defined that consumes AuthContext and returns its value with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a custom useAuth hook that properly consumes the AuthContext. This will make it much easier to access authentication state and functions throughout your app.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there are a few issues. Make sure your hook is named useAuth, uses useContext with AuthContext, and returns the context value. Also ensure it has proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useAuth hook isn't quite right. You need to create a function named useAuth that uses useContext with AuthContext and returns its value. Remember to add proper TypeScript typing.

steps.title: Create a LoginButton component
steps.instruction: Define a functional component named LoginButton that uses the useAuth hook to access authentication state and functions.
steps.hint: Create a new component that returns JSX. Inside it, call useAuth() to get the auth context values.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new LoginButton component that uses the useAuth hook (even though useAuth is not yet defined - we'll define it in the next step).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the LoginButton component structure. Next we'll define the useAuth hook so it can actually provide the auth context.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started creating the component, but make sure it's named LoginButton and uses the useAuth hook.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should be named LoginButton and use the useAuth hook to access authentication context.

steps.title: Implement LoginButton logic and JSX
steps.instruction: Inside the LoginButton component, add conditional rendering that shows a welcome message when authenticated and a login button when not authenticated. The login button's onClick should call the login function from context.
steps.hint: Use the useAuth hook to get isAuthenticated and login. Return JSX with a ternary operator: if isAuthenticated is true, show a welcome message; otherwise, show a button with onClick={login}.
steps.expectedOutcome: The LoginButton component will display a welcome message when the user is authenticated, and a login button when not authenticated. Clicking the login button will trigger the login function from context.
successCriteria: Uses useAuth hook to get context values
Shows welcome message when isAuthenticated is true
Shows button with onClick={login} when isAuthenticated is false
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the LoginButton component with conditional rendering. It now displays appropriate UI based on authentication state and the login button is properly wired to the context login function.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there are some issues. Make sure you're using the useAuth hook to get both isAuthenticated and login, and that your conditional rendering properly shows the welcome message when authenticated and the login button when not.
steps.feedbackWrong: The LoginButton component doesn't have the required conditional rendering logic. Remember to use the useAuth hook to access context values and implement a ternary operator to show different UI based on isAuthenticated.
